cells.tense: You are reading what's fair while the moment is still going on.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Pick the thing between you and someone else that's already over. Say the one closing sentence this week, and mean it as the end of it.
cells.core:
You can call what's fair in real time. Something lands between you and another person and the judgment shows up while the exchange is still moving — no waiting a day to find out what you actually felt. The read arrives the same hour the words do.

Sitting with this among other people isn't simple. There's a version where every exchange gets a small verdict, and the verdict holds you a beat longer than the moment needs. Nothing here is being asked of you that you'd have to build first. Take a finished thing, close it in one sentence, and go on to the next. Not a new habit — the door you're standing in.
cells.sheetLine: You can call what's fair while it's still happening.
cells.verb: Weighing what is fair between people while the moment is still open.
cells.place: Where what you are stops being private and starts showing at the table.

cells.tense: You will be running the tally before anyone has said a word.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: For one week carry what is actually yours — a household, a shift, one bill — and leave other people's side of it alone. At week's end, settle anything still open, once.
cells.core:
The account keeps running while the conversation is happening. Every exchange gets weighed before it's over — who gave what, who owes, whether it matches last time — and next week's words get balanced while this week's are still being said. The scale runs constantly, and it costs you the ease you want.

The strength under this doesn't have to squeeze anything. Carry one thing, all of it, and nothing else. Drop the running total for seven days. If someone comes up short, you'll know at the end without having watched for it, and you can settle it once and be done. Fairness doesn't need the ledger kept in the open to stay fair.
cells.sheetLine: The tally doesn't have to run every minute.

cells.tense: You were the one who found the fair answer, and you are still outside it.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Take a stuck situation and write what happened, in sequence, with no feeling words in it. When the page is done, read it once and set it down.
cells.core:
The fair reading comes, and by the time it arrives the moment has already closed over. You have the answer, and you're a beat behind where it was needed. Something in the timing is off — the exchange is finished and you're still holding the version you'd have said, so it keeps not settling.

Coming back doesn't start with more feeling. It starts with a page. Pick something you can't decide about and write the facts down in sequence, the way a clerk would, no feeling words at all. Read it once and set it down. Your read is accurate — it only needed a surface outside your head to land on. One page, one pass, and you're describing the thing instead of hovering next to it.
cells.sheetLine: Your read is accurate. It just needs a surface.

cells.tense: You are being fair with people right now, and the fairness is credited to the situation.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Next charged moment with someone, look first: what was said, before your read. Answer it. Then, alone, notice anything in that exchange that was yours.
cells.core:
The right call comes out of you before you've said it's yours. Something heated comes up with another person, and your fair read arrives in the same breath — you're deciding and it doesn't feel like deciding. The credit for it is landing on the situation instead of on you.

What you need here is smaller than what you're handling now. The next live moment, look at what was actually said before you reach for the judgment. Then answer. Later, by yourself, put your finger on anything in that exchange that was yours. First you look, then you answer, then you say that part was mine — in that order and not another.
cells.sheetLine: The fair read is already yours. Claim it as yours.
cells.verb: Weighing what is fair between people while the moment is still open.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: 'you'd have said you were just going along with it' in the Unacknowledged cell puts a self-account in the person's mouth, which is exactly the line the rules draw; I've recast it so the reading simply reports the attribution landing under circumstance, which the record itself names ('authorship misattributed') — the person stays free to say no and still keep the ask. The likely objection in the Balanced cell is that 'mediating' isn't a thing this person does and 'not being asked to build it' is flattery, so I anchored it in what can be seen (the moment passing while the answer is still being weighed) rather than an identity claim. Each ask survives my read being wrong because it is a gesture anyone can perform once and watch, and each teaches something even if the status is off — none of them promises to fix anything. The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'mediating between what's said and what's felt' line; I kept it as a single clause and gave it no work to do after that, so if it isn't theirs the reading still stands on the ask. Ask 1 uses 'release what is done and keep what serves' done small as a single unwritten sentence rather than a week-long practice, so it doesn't require the person to remember anything; ask 4 reduces authorship to naming in the moment only, per the REDUCTION mechanism, and does not ask them to account for the past. For Too Little I pulled energy through Executor of Cognition rather than pushing feeling into the empty seat, so the ask is a written fact-list, not an emotional exercise.
